items.stem: As a result of the Mexican–American War, all of the following became part of the United States EXCEPT
options: California
Nevada
New Mexico
Texas
items.explanation: Texas was annexed by the United States in 1845, prior to the start of the Mexican–American War. All the other territories mentioned in the answer choices came to the United States as a result of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ended the war.

option_explanations.A: California came to the United States through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848), which ended the Mexican-American War — so it was a result of the war, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Nevada was part of the Mexican Cession transferred by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) — a result of the war, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: New Mexico was part of the Mexican Cession transferred by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) — a result of the war, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Texas was annexed by the United States in 1845, before the Mexican-American War began in 1846. Its annexation helped cause the war; it was not gained as a result of it.

items.stem: “Bleeding Kansas” was a direct result of the doctrine of
options: judicial review
imperialism
containment
popular sovereignty
items.explanation: The term “Bleeding Kansas” refers to the battle in Kansas between proslavery and abolitionist forces. The doctrine of popular sovereignty had created the circumstances that led to the gruesome conflict; it left the slave status of each territory up to its residents, to be decided at the time when the territory was ready to write a constitution and apply for statehood. Both sides wanted Kansas badly, and both sent representatives into the territory to form governments. President Pierce recognized the proslavery government, but abolitionist forces cried “foul” and continued their fight to establish Kansas as a free state. More than 200 people died in the resulting skirmishes.

option_explanations.A: Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws as unconstitutional. It had nothing to do with the violence in Kansas.
option_explanations.B: Imperialism — building overseas empires — is the wrong concept and the wrong era for a conflict over slavery in a western territory in the 1850s.
option_explanations.C: Containment was the Cold War doctrine for checking Soviet expansion, nearly a century later. It is anachronistic here.
option_explanations.D: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) applied popular sovereignty to Kansas, letting settlers decide on slavery. Proslavery and antislavery settlers flooded in, set up rival governments, and fought — 'Bleeding Kansas.'

items.stem: Which of the following was a confederate advantage during the Civil War?
options: Greater familiarity with battlegrounds
Better organized state governments
Superior transportation systems
A larger fighting force
items.explanation: Most of the Civil War, particularly in the later stages, was fought on southern territory. This homeland advantage was one of the few relative strengths the South had when fighting the wealthier, more populous, and better organized North.

option_explanations.A: Most of the war was fought on Southern soil, so Confederate armies knew the terrain and fought defensively on home ground — one of the South's few real advantages against a wealthier, more populous North.
option_explanations.B: The Confederacy's state governments were less organized and less centralized than the Union's; its states'-rights ethos actually hampered coordination.
option_explanations.C: Transportation was a Northern advantage. The North had the denser railroad network and better supply systems; the South's were sparse and deteriorating.
option_explanations.D: The North had the larger fighting force — roughly two-to-one or more in manpower — thanks to its much bigger population. Numbers were a Union advantage, not a Confederate one.

options: he refused to carry out Lincoln’s plan for reconstruction
he vetoed the Wade-Davis Bill
Congress was controlled by Republicans and he was a Democrat
he violated the Tenure of Office Act by firing Secretary of War Stanton
items.explanation: Many historians argue that Andrew Johnson was neither the man nor the politician that Lincoln was. Johnson locked horns with the Radical Republicans in Congress over several issues pertaining to Reconstruction. Johnson had vetoed the Tenure of Office Act, which required a president to obtain Senate approval before firing an appointed official. The Senate argued that if it had the power to confirm nominations, it should also be allowed to have a say in the event a president wanted to fire someone. Congress overrode Johnson’s veto; Johnson fired his secretary of war, the Radical Republican Edwin Stanton; and the House of Representatives impeached the president of the United States for the first time in American history. Johnson was acquitted, however, by one vote in the Senate and thus remained in office to finish his term.

option_explanations.A: Lincoln was assassinated before he could carry out a Reconstruction plan, so there was no 'Lincoln's plan' for Johnson to refuse. Johnson clashed with Congress's Radical Republicans, and the impeachment rested on a specific legal charge.
option_explanations.B: The Wade-Davis Bill (1864) was pocket-vetoed by Lincoln, not Johnson. It belongs to Lincoln's presidency, not Johnson's.
option_explanations.C: Republican control of Congress was the political backdrop, but impeachment required a legal charge — party arithmetic alone was not the stated cause.
option_explanations.D: Johnson fired Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act, which barred the president from removing Senate-confirmed officials without Senate approval. The House impeached him for it; the Senate fell one vote short of conviction.

items.stem: The dispute over electoral votes in the election of 1876
options: was similar to the election of 2000 in that the Supreme Court ultimately had to step in and decide the election
was resolved by a special bipartisan commission and resulted in the end of military reconstruction
led many members of Congress to push for a Constitutional amendment to abolish the Electoral College
was resolved when Samuel J. Tilden conceded the election to Rutherford
items.explanation: The election of 1876 is another of the disputed elections in American political history. Although Samuel J. Tilden, then governor of New York, won the popular vote nationwide, there were several states that contested the results of the election. Consequently, a special bipartisan commission was set up to determine the outcome of the election. In what became known as the “Compromise of 1877,” Rutherford B. Hayes won the presidential election by a margin of one single electoral vote. Hayes had promised to remove federal troops still stationed in the South after the Civil War, thus ending military reconstruction.

option_explanations.A: The Supreme Court did not decide the 1876 election — that parallel fits 2000 (Bush v. Gore). In 1876 Congress created a special electoral commission instead.
option_explanations.B: A 15-member bipartisan commission awarded the disputed electoral votes to Rutherford B. Hayes. In the Compromise of 1877, Hayes took the presidency by a single electoral vote and in return withdrew the remaining federal troops from the South, ending military Reconstruction.
option_explanations.C: The disputed election did not produce a serious push to abolish the Electoral College; the system remained in place.
option_explanations.D: Samuel J. Tilden never conceded. He won the national popular vote and contested the result to the end; the commission's decision, not a concession, settled it.

items.stem: Following the Civil War, most freed enslaved people
options: stayed in the South and worked as sharecroppers
joined the pioneering movement as it headed West
moved to the North to work in factories
took work building the nation’s growing railroad system
items.explanation: Remember that most enslaved people had no job skills and could neither read nor write. They had no money and nowhere to go when slavery was abolished. Some enslaved people took off in search of their scattered families, but most stayed exactly where they were and worked as tenant farmers or sharecroppers. Under the new wage-labor system, plantations were subdivided into smaller farms of 30 to 50 acres, which were then leased to freedmen under a one-year contract. Tenants would work a piece of land and turn over 50 percent of their crops to the landlord. Often, other expenses, such as rent for a run-down shack or over-priced groceries, available only through the landowner, would be deducted from whatever was produced. One of the services initially provided by the Freedmen’s Bureau was to help freed enslaved people who could neither read nor write understand the contracts they were about to sign. The system of sharecropping persisted well into the 20th century, keeping many Black people in positions of poverty and degradation. Choice (C) is incorrect for reasons stated above. The Great Migration of southern Black people into northern cities did not take place until World War I, long after Reconstruction. Choice (D) is incorrect because Chinese immigrants were used to construct the nation’s railroad system, much of which was built during and just after the war (the transcontinental line was completed in 1869).

option_explanations.A: Most freed people had no money, no land, and often could not read or write. They stayed where they were and worked as sharecroppers or tenant farmers, typically surrendering half their crop to the landlord under one-year contracts.
option_explanations.B: The westward pioneer movement was overwhelmingly white. Few freed people had the means to head west; the Exoduster migration to Kansas did not come until 1879 and involved a minority.
option_explanations.C: The move to Northern factories was the Great Migration, which began around World War I — half a century later, not the immediate postwar pattern.
option_explanations.D: Railroad construction crews were largely Irish and Chinese immigrant laborers. Freed people generally lacked the mobility and resources to take up railroad work.

items.stem: The Know-Nothing Party focused its efforts almost exclusively on the issue of
options: the right to bear arms
the prohibition of alcohol
women’s rights
immigration
items.explanation: The Know-Nothings were a nativist group formed in response to the growing concentration of immigrants—particularly Irish and German Catholics—in Eastern cities. The party grew out of a number of secret societies whose members were instructed to tell outsiders nothing, hence the party’s name. When asked anything about their groups, Know-Nothings would respond, “I know nothing.” Their program included a 25-year residency requirement for citizenship; they also wanted to restrict all public offices to only those who were native-born Americans. By 1855, they had changed their name to the American Party, and in 1856, they fielded a presidential candidate (former president Millard Fillmore). Within a few years, the party had disbanded, destroyed by their disagreements over slavery. Most northern Know-Nothings joined the Republican Party.

option_explanations.A: The right to bear arms was not the Know-Nothings' cause. They were nativists focused on immigration, not on gun rights.
option_explanations.B: Prohibition of alcohol was the temperance movement's cause — a separate reform effort, not the Know-Nothing program.
option_explanations.C: Women's rights belonged to the Seneca Falls and suffrage movements, not to the Know-Nothings.
option_explanations.D: The Know-Nothing (American) Party was a nativist movement reacting against Irish and German Catholic immigration. It demanded a long residency requirement for citizenship and public office reserved for the native-born.

items.stem: The Free-Soil Party advocated which of the following?
options: The freedom of settlers within the territories to determine the slave status of their new state
The passage of the Homestead Act to give free land to all Western settlers
The exclusion of slavery from any of the new territories
The policy of giving newly freed enslaved people “40 acres and a mule” following the Civil War
items.explanation: The Free-Soil Party was created in the mid-1840s and was more like a faction or interest group than a political party. However, unlike a faction, it developed a political platform and nominated a candidate (Martin Van Buren) for the presidential election of 1848. The Free-Soil Party attracted antislavery “Conscience” Whigs, former members of the Liberty Party, and pro-Wilmot Proviso Democrats. The Wilmot Proviso was rejected by Congress but suggested that there be no slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico. Free-Soilers were opposed to the extension of slavery into the new territories. Remember, the Constitution protected slavery where it already existed, but many people believed Congress could prevent the further spread of slavery as the United States acquired new land. Although the Free-Soil Party did not exist for long, its major principles were adopted by the new Republican Party, which was formed in 1854 and was opposed to the extension of slavery into the new territories.

option_explanations.A: Letting settlers decide slavery's status was popular sovereignty — the Democrats' doctrine and the opposite of what Free-Soilers wanted.
option_explanations.B: The Homestead Act (1862) came much later, during the Civil War under a Republican Congress — not part of the Free-Soil platform of the 1840s.
option_explanations.C: The Free-Soil Party (1848) stood for keeping slavery out of the new western territories — 'free soil, free labor, free men' — drawing on the Wilmot Proviso's idea that the Mexican Cession should be free.
option_explanations.D: 'Forty acres and a mule' was a postwar Reconstruction proposal (Sherman's Field Order 15, 1865), two decades after the Free-Soil Party's founding.

items.stem: The principle of popular sovereignty stated that
options: whenever a new area was settled, all United States citizens were required to vote on the slave status of that area
slavery would not be permitted in any area after 1848
the president, after meeting with public interest groups, was to decide on whether enslaved people would be allowed in a given territory
settlers in the Western territories, not Congress, would decide whether to allow slavery in their territories
items.explanation: In the election of 1848, the Democrats realized that their party was crumbling because its members could not agree on whether to allow slavery in the Western territories. They sought a policy to appease both abolitionists and slaveholders; the result of that search was the concept of popular sovereignty. By allowing the settlers to decide the slave status of an area, popular sovereignty took some pressure off Congress, which was growing increasingly divided over the issue. It also took pressure off the political parties, which were coming apart because of the irreconcilable regional differences of their members. Henry Clay invoked the notion of popular sovereignty in the Compromise of 1850, but the compromise contained a purposefully ambiguous interpretation of what popular sovereignty meant. While the ambiguous wording was necessary to make the Compromise of 1850 possible, it also made future disagreements over the issue inevitable.

option_explanations.A: Popular sovereignty did not give every U.S. citizen a vote on a territory's status. The decision belonged to the territory's own settlers.
option_explanations.B: Popular sovereignty did not ban slavery after 1848 — it permitted slavery wherever the settlers chose it.
option_explanations.C: The president did not decide. The whole point of the doctrine was to move the decision out of Washington entirely and hand it to the settlers.
option_explanations.D: Popular sovereignty, championed by Lewis Cass and Stephen Douglas, held that the settlers of each Western territory — not Congress — would vote on whether to allow slavery there.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement set by the Reconstruction Act of 1867 for southern states’ readmission to the Union?
options: Black people had to be allowed to participate in state conventions and state elections.
The state had to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution.
The state had to pay reparations and provide land grants to all former enslaved people.
The state had to rewrite its constitution and ratify it.
items.explanation: The Reconstruction Act of 1867, Congress’s plan for the rehabilitation of the South, was much harsher than President Johnson’s plan. Johnson, like Lincoln (who began planning the method for readmitting southern states before his assassination), wanted a reconciliatory plan that punished only the most prominent leaders of the secession. Radical Republicans in Congress wanted something much tougher, and Johnson’s plan was so lenient (in the first postwar Congress, Johnson’s plan would have allowed the former president of the Confederacy to take a seat in the Senate) that it drove many moderates into the radicals’ camp. The result was the Reconstruction Act, a punitive measure that imposed a number of strict requirements on southern states as preconditions for their readmission to the Union. Choices (A), (B), and (D) list all of those preconditions; the fact that Congress did not impose any requirements such as the one described in (C) pretty much doomed postwar southern Black people to poverty.

option_explanations.A: This was a genuine requirement: the Reconstruction Act of 1867 required Black participation in the state conventions and elections that would frame the new governments.
option_explanations.B: This was a genuine requirement: readmission was conditioned on ratifying the Fourteenth Amendment.
option_explanations.C: Congress never required readmitted states to pay reparations or grant land to former enslaved people. 'Forty acres and a mule' was proposed but never enacted as a condition of readmission.
option_explanations.D: This was a genuine requirement: each state had to write a new constitution and have it ratified.

items.stem: Which battle gave Lincoln the victory he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation?
options: Gettysburg
Antietam
Fort Sumter
Harper’s Ferry
items.explanation: In September of 1862, the Battle of Antietam gave President Lincoln the victory he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation from a position of apparent strength. Because the confederates had been advancing north up until that time, Lincoln feared that issuing the Proclamation without a clear victory would seem like a desperate act. The Emancipation Proclamation was issued four months later in January of 1863.

option_explanations.A: Gettysburg (July 1863) came six months after the Emancipation Proclamation took effect (January 1863) — too late to have enabled it.
option_explanations.B: Antietam (September 17, 1862) gave Lincoln the Union victory he needed. He issued the preliminary Proclamation on September 22, with emancipation to take effect January 1, 1863.
option_explanations.C: Fort Sumter (April 1861) was the war's opening battle — nearly two years before the Proclamation, not the victory that made it politically possible.
option_explanations.D: Harpers Ferry was John Brown's 1859 raid, before the war began. It was not a Union battlefield victory at all.
